gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, of its five picks, only the WEN units have a 240 V parallel path documented by the maker: WEN's GNA240i kit links two 240V WEN inverters through a transfer-switch-ready 14-50R rated 50 A / 12,000 W, and works only with 240V WEN models that have three parallel ports, not 120V-only units or 120V ports. WEN's other kit, the GNA50i, outputs 120 V only, and Champion lists 'Parallel capability: No' for the 201417, ChatGPT's 'best dual-fuel' pick.
standout_why: I compared against Lights On Labs (cited), homewelder.com (rank 1) and Consumer Reports (cited). Lights On Labs mentions parallel only for the 120V-only Honda EU2200i ('Two can run in parallel with Honda's kit'). For the EU7000iS it says only that the 30 A locking outlet 'feeds a transfer switch or interlock kit'. It never says whether any 120/240V pick can be paralleled at 240 V, and it doesn't mention neutral bonding. homewelder.com lists L14-30R/14-50R outlets but says nothing on parallel kits, neutral bonding or transfer switches. The Consumer Reports page returned only category navigation with no specs. ChatGPT's own answer doesn't address parallel capability at all.
decides: For a shopper who may later need more 240 V power than one unit gives (well pump plus central AC, or a 50 A EV/panel feed), this changes the pick. The WEN TF1050iX or DF680iX can be doubled at 240 V with the $72.69 GNA240i (12,000 W through one 14-50R). The Champion 201417 cannot be paralleled at all per Champion's spec table. WEN's 120V kit (GNA50i) would drop a WEN pair to 120 V only, so buying the wrong kit loses split phase. WEN also states both of its units have a bonded neutral, which the installer needs to know when choosing the transfer switch or interlock. For one-generator buyers it confirms ChatGPT's watts-per-dollar ranking but adds a reason to prefer WEN over Champion if expansion matters. The Westinghouse ecoGen10000 is $1,299 and listed as unavailable on Westinghouse's own store, not the $1,149 ChatGPT showed.
